newsitem.title: JAPAN: Big Japan banks to use new accounting method.
newsitem.headline: Big Japan banks to use new accounting method.

text.p: Twenty-nine of Japan's biggest banks plan to adopt a new accounting method for their short-term trading accounts starting from the current business year, the Ministry of Finance said on Tuesday.

The ministry said the banks had been given permission to use the new accounting method after parliament passed a special act last June allowing banks and brokerages to include gains or losses from derivatives and short-term securities trading in income statements from the end of the 1997/98 fiscal year.
In mark-to-market accounting, unrealised gains or losses in trading accounts must be included in operating profits or losses in current income statements.

A MOF official said the banks included the nation's top 10 nationwide commercial banks, three long-term credit banks, six major trust banks, excluding Nippon Trust Bank Ltd, and the trust banking subsidiaries of Nomura Securities Co Ltd and Daiwa Securities Co Ltd.

Among regional banks, Bank of Yokohama Ltd, Chiba Bank Ltd, Joyo Bank Ltd, Shizuoka Bank Ltd, Hokuriku Bank Ltd and Hiroshima Bank Ltd will use the new accounting method along with Bank of Nagoya, a second-tier regional bank.
Norinchukin Bank, a central bank for agricultural financial firms, also plans to use the new method.
If other Japanese banks intend to introduce the new accounting measure, the MOF may permit them to do so beginning from the 1998/99 business year, the official said.
Japanese banks using the new accounting method separate their short-term trading accounts from their long-term holdings, he said.

Currently in Japan, financial products are basically appraised according to the cost of purchase, and realised gains or losses are posted in current income statements only when the positions are closed.
Banking industry sources said that while the use of mark-to-market accounting would help increase arbitrage deals in derivatives, it would not have any major impact on banks' business results.

Nine foreign banks in Japan also told the ministry they plan to introduce the new accounting method from 1997/98. Foreign banks in Japan do not need to receive permission from the ministry to do so, the official said.
The nine include Citibank N.A., Chase Manhattan Bank N.A., and Bank of America NT & Sa.
